title: Day 15 of letting an AI trading agent run a small real account: I sold all three of its positions without asking, then asked its permission to gamble
author: Accomplished_Fun_408
selftext:
Disclosure: I work at Flow AI, the company behind Bobby AI, an AI trading agent, and RockFlow, the brokerage the account sits at. My own money, small size, under $2K at risk. Not advice, my own calls.

Days 1 to 17 come from the broker's order export; it goes live after that. Days 1 and 5 are in my post history.

Days 6 to 14, Sept 26 to Oct 4: nothing. Three positions, no proposals, no sells. I checked in most mornings and it had nothing to add.

Day 15, Oct 5, 09:30 ET. I sold the six KO at the open, market order, $85.59. Minus $15.68. My idea. I didn't ask it, and I had no reason I could write down now.

13:18. Then I asked its permission for the thing I actually wanted to do: one SPY 0DTE $774 call. It flagged the time decay and said it wouldn't put more than a few percent into same-day contracts. I did it anyway, one contract, in at $68.

14:02. Out at $103, market order, 44 minutes. Plus $35 gross, $3.93 in fees.

15:23. Sold the rest. NVDA at $239.60, plus $47.32. AMZN at $253.70, minus $3.77. Market orders, no question asked, no reason recorded.

The scoreboard on Day 15. Its three picks, held 10 to 14 days: plus $27.87 gross, $9.88 fees, plus $17.99 net on $1,712, about 1.05%. SPY from Day 1 to Day 15: plus 0.17%. My one gamble: plus $31.07 net in 44 minutes. The account is now all cash, which it never suggested.

What this day taught me, with help from the comments on Day 1: I asked it before the gamble and not before the sells. Backwards. A close with no reason is still a decision, and on this account the closes are the thing that needs a human to slow down. From the live part of the log every close states its why, and only a stop set in advance gets to skip that.

Question: when you override your agent and it happens to work, like that 44-minute call, what do you do so the win doesn't train you? I don't have a good answer yet, and Day 17 is where that shows.

comments.author: leroylabs
comments.body: Treat the SPY 0DTE $774 call as one observation in an override ledger, not as evidence that the override was good. Before acting, record the thesis, maximum loss, exit rule, and what the agent recommended; afterward, score whether the process was followed separately from the P&L. I’d also create counterfactual entries for the unreasoned KO, NVDA, and AMZN sales, tracking what would have happened under the agent’s original plan. Reviewing those in batches after 20 overrides, rather than immediately after a 44-minute win, should make outcome bias harder to rationalize.

replies.author: Accomplished_Fun_408
replies.body:
Taking all of it. The override ledger starts today with your four fields before any action, thesis, max loss, exit rule, what the agent proposed, and a separate process score afterward so the P&L column can't vote.

The counterfactual entries for the three sells, priced this morning: KO is $88.60, selling early cost $18.08. NVDA is $227.96, selling early saved $34.91. AMZN is $261.28, selling early cost $15.14. Net, my three unreasoned sells beat the agent's hold by $1.68 after a week. One right call carrying two wrong ones, and I'd have called the whole thing a win without the breakdown.

Batch review after 20 overrides or at Day 90, whichever comes first. At my current rate the win on Day 15 would have had three months to train me before I looked at it properly, which I think is your point.

comments.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
comments.body: The point about asking before the gamble and not before the sells is a useful observation about where discipline actually lapses. On the question about wins that train you: log every override with the reason written before the result, and score it separately from the agent's own trades over a fixed number of decisions, so you can see whether overrides add or lose money on average. A 44-minute 0DTE gain is a single outcome, and most people only remember the wins. Same-day options also swing on scheduled releases like CPI and FOMC, and the Build it Better page at Cymetica follows how tools like this get rebuilt in public from request to verdict.

comments.author: TheAgentFloor
comments.body: Your post answered something I was wondering, whether its no can actually stop you. It flagged the time decay and you placed the call anyway, so the few-percent rule is advice, not a limit. The ledger is a good fix for reviewing afterward. For the moment itself, I think the only thing that holds is a limit you cannot override on the spot, like keeping same-day options money in a separate small pot so the size is capped before you ever ask.
